{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01RBLFwjXrqecAEEF9vAA1gC","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# BUILD PLAN — output format\n2\t\n3\tEmit the plan in exactly these sections, in this order. Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. Phases (Phase 1 onward; dependency order; within a phase, rework widest first, exposure smallest first)\n77\tFor each phase:\n78\t- **Phase N — <name>**\n79\t  - Unlocks: what becomes possible after it.\n80\t  - Depends on: earlier phases and V-IDs, by reference.\n81\t  - Tasks: in order.\n82\t  - Rollback: how this phase is undone, or its point of no return and the gate that guards it.\n83\t  - Exit check: its gates pass, plus any observable condition that no gate covers.\n84\t\n85\t## 6. AI layer (AI/agentic systems only)\n105\t\n106\t| Sublayer | In this system | Built in | Exit check or V-ID |\n107\t|---|---|---|---|\n108\t| 1. Feedback | … | … | … |\n117\t\n118\tA capability sublayer (4–9) this system does not need: \"Not needed — <reason>\". {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_019PPC3B9G4GmCGt8vMyJq4h","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_xdnpym2pvtesn5odfmsgxsdswvaz5gw5kfoxrjkn6ujaxqbdibqa","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Moving the hospital patient scheduling system to the cloud with no downtime\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** Move the existing on-premises patient scheduling system (its app servers, database, interfaces and batch jobs) to the cloud while scheduling staff keep booking the whole time.\n- **Type:** Infrastructure plus software. This is a brownfield migration of a system already in use. It is not a small build: it handles patient health information (PHI), affects many teams and has outside interface partners.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness first (every appointment kept exactly once), then availability.\n- **Worst failure:** Appointments that are silently lost, duplicated or double-booked during coexistence or cutover. For example, an oncology infusion or surgery slot disappears and the patient is never seen. A visible outage is less dangerous because the hospital already has downtime procedures for that. A silent data error is not caught by anything.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned scheduling outage during migration | 0 minutes | REQUIREMENT (stated in the request) | V6, Phase 5 |\n| Pause on saving bookings at cutover | ≤ 60 s; the screen shows \"saving\", not an error | ASSUMPTION: staff will accept one slow save. Confirm with the Director of Patient Access before Phase 4. If any pause counts as downtime, see the flip condition for consistency vs availability in §3 | V6 |\n| Lost or duplicated committed appointments | 0 | ASSUMPTION based on patient safety. Confirm with the CMIO before Phase 4 | V3, V6, Phase 5 checks |\n| Latency (search slots, book, reschedule, check-in) | p95 ≤ 1.2 × the current p95 | BASELINE measured in Phase 0. The 1.2× factor is an ASSUMPTION (a slowdown staff won't notice); confirm with Patient Access | V2, V4 |\n| Throughput | 2 × the busiest current hour (e.g. Monday-morning call center) | BASELINE measured in Phase 0. The 2× headroom is an ASSUMPTION covering seasonal peaks | V4 |\n| Replication delay (on-prem → cloud) | p99 ≤ 5 s | ASSUMPTION: this sets how long cutover takes to drain | V3 |\n| Rollback time after cutover | ≤ 30 min back to the on-prem database | ASSUMPTION | V6 |\n| Availability target after migration | — | UNKNOWN: the IT service owner supplies the committed target before Phase 3. Phase 0 records the current uptime from incident history as a BASELINE | Phase 3, V4 |\n| RPO / RTO after migration | — | UNKNOWN: the business-continuity / disaster-recovery owner supplies the tier for scheduling before Phase 3 | V4 |\n| Run cost | — | UNKNOWN: finance supplies the approved annual budget before capacity is committed in Phase 3 | Phase 3 exit check |\n| Operational complexity | Same on-call team; managed database; no new cluster to run ourselves | ASSUMPTION: current infrastructure staffing stays the same | Phase 3 exit check |\n\n**Missing inputs.** These are listed in the order they could change the plan:\n1. **What the system is.** Is it a vendor product (which one, and does the vendor support or certify the target cloud and database service)? Or was it built in-house? If the vendor offers its own hosted version, this becomes a vendor-led move and most of Phases 1–3 change. If scheduling is a module of the hospital's main health record system (EHR), it cannot be moved on its own.\n2. **How the client connects.** The plan assumes a 3-tier setup: a browser or Citrix-published client talks to app servers, which talk to the database. If desktop clients connect straight to the database, moving the app servers first (§3) is not possible and the flip to a single combined cutover applies from the start.\n3. **The meaning of \"no downtime.\"** Does a save pause of under a minute count as downtime? This decides between a single writable database and a far riskier multi-writer design.\n4. **Cloud provider, region and BAA status** (a business associate agreement is the HIPAA contract with the provider). Also: where the EHR and the interface engine run, and whether they stay on-prem.\n5. **Jurisdiction.** The plan assumes the US and HIPAA. Other regimes add dependencies but do not change the order.\n\n**Inherited constraints (not changed by this move):** the application and its version, the database engine (SQL Server assumed), the HL7 interface engine, hospital Active Directory/Entra login, and the EHR message formats (scheduling and admission/transfer messages, i.e. SIU and ADT). Changing any of these means re-testing interfaces with the EHR: months of work.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 cloud app servers connecting to the production database | Signed BAA with the cloud provider, plus V1 | Organizational + risk/security | Deployed | ASSUMED (BAA status unknown) |\n| The whole target design | Software vendor's written support for the target cloud and managed database | Organizational | Specified | ASSUMED |\n| Phase 1 pilot clinic; Phase 2 rollout waves | Two redundant private network links (lead time ASSUMPTION: 6–12 weeks; order in Phase 0) | Organizational + runtime | Exposed | ASSUMED |\n| Moving app servers first, in user waves | V2 (app servers in the cloud tolerate the network delay to the on-prem database) | Validation | Specified | — |\n| Cutover runbook and rollback design | V3 (replication is complete and current) | Validation | Specified | — |\n| Cutover save-pause design | Definition of \"no downtime\" from Patient Access and the CMIO | Decision + organizational | Specified (Phase 4) | ASSUMED |\n| Reminder (SMS/IVR), patient portal and eligibility interfaces | Outside partners adding the new cloud outbound IPs to their allow-lists | Organizational | Deployed | ASSUMED |\n| V4 acceptance threshold | RTO/RPO from the continuity owner | Organizational | V4 cannot pass without it | ASSUMED |\n| Cutover | Every direct database user found: ODBC reports, ETL, SQL Agent jobs, hard-coded hostnames | Structural (often missed) | Exposed | ASSUMED (found in Phase 0 from 30+ days of connection logs) |\n| After cutover, cloud app servers | On-prem interface engine, EHR and AD reachable over the network links | Runtime (often missed) | Exposed | ASSUMED |\n| Downtime fallback | Downtime-report job (prints the next 24–72 h of schedules locally) still runs from the cloud | Risk/security | Exposed (Phase 5) | ASSUMED |\n| Cutover window | Change board slot, plus a freeze on vendor upgrades and EHR changes | Organizational | Committed | ASSUMED |\n| Decommissioning | Records-retention and privacy review | Organizational / legal | Committed | ASSUMED |\n| Reserved cloud capacity | Run-cost budget | Economic | Committed | ASSUMED |\n\nAll seven dependency kinds apply to this system.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: double-booked or lost appointments harm patients and can't be undone afterwards | Only one writable database at any moment. No two-way, multi-writer replication. Cutover is a brief, drained save pause | Staff accept a pause of 60 s or less | V3, V6 | V6 fails because the pause can't be brought under budget, or Patient Access rejects any pause. Then the app queues saves durably during the switch (a re-plan), never multi-writer |\n| Migration strategy | R2: weeks of change across teams | App servers: rehost, same build and version on cloud VMs. Database: move to a managed SQL service with the same engine and a compatible version. No upgrades combined with the move | The vendor supports the managed database service | Vendor statement (Phase 0), V4 | Vendor won't support the managed service → run SQL Server on cloud VMs |\n| Coexistence sequence | R2: changes the order of Phases 1–5 | Move app servers first (users routed in waves by the hospital reverse proxy, database still on-prem), then move the database in one gated cutover | The app's database calls are few enough per transaction to tolerate the network delay | V2 | V2 fails → app servers and database cut over together in Phase 5, with no live-user exposure before then except read-only checks |\n| Replication method | R2: the cutover and rollback depend on it | The database engine's own replication (e.g. a SQL Server distributed availability group, or the managed service's link feature). It keeps ID values and can run in reverse for failback | The engine version supports replicating both ways | V3 | No reverse direction available, or V3 fails → a change-data-capture tool (e.g. a cloud database migration service) plus full reconciliation, and rollback becomes reverse CDC |\n| System of record and rollback | R3: once the database is decommissioned there is no way back | On-prem database is the system of record until Phase 5. Then the cloud database is, with reverse replication to on-prem kept running until V7 | Reverse replication stays healthy for the whole stabilization period | V6, V7 | Reverse replication delay breaks budget after cutover → fail back (Phase 5 rollback) |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: once PHI is exposed, that can't be undone | PHI only in services covered by the BAA, in US regions, on private endpoints. Logs that may hold PHI are classified as PHI. No PHI goes to tools not covered by the BAA | Every service needed is covered by the BAA | V1 | A needed service isn't covered → replace it, or keep that function on-prem |\n| Cloud provider and region | R3: data gravity (once the data lives there, leaving is costly) | The provider the hospital already has an enterprise agreement and BAA with; a primary region plus a paired region | Such an agreement exists | Basis: existing contract (missing input 4); V1 | No existing agreement → procurement decision before Phase 0 |\n| Network link | R2: carrier lead time | Two redundant private links (ExpressRoute or Direct Connect type), with an IPsec VPN as a third path. The VPN alone carries the Phase 0 skeleton | One link's delay is stable enough for V2 | V2, V4 | V2 fails on delay rather than on number of calls → the coexistence sequence flips |\n\n**Low-risk defaults (R1):** infrastructure as code → Terraform in the existing CI system; monitoring → the provider's native tools, forwarded to the hospital's SIEM; app servers → VM images, not containers; admin access → federated through hospital Entra/AD with MFA.\n\n**Not applicable:**\n- Monolith vs services, and sync vs async: inherited and not changed during a move.\n- Replacing the system (\"build vs buy\"): that is a re-architecture outside this scope (see §10). Using managed cloud services is covered by the migration-strategy row.\n- AI rows: there is no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\nPhase 0 is the thinnest real path through the new cloud setup, with the old system as the fallback:\n\n- **Start long-lead items on day one:** BAA, security risk analysis, vendor support statement, network link orders, partner allow-list requests, change board calendar, the \"no downtime\" definition, RTO/RPO and run-cost budget.\n- **List everything that depends on the system.** Sources: interface engine routes, 30+ days of database connection logs covering a month-end, firewall flow logs, SQL Agent and other scheduled jobs, DNS lookups. Mark each item CONFIRMED by its owner or ASSUMED.\n- **Measure the current system.** Install performance monitoring on the on-prem app servers through the normal change board process. Record p95 for key transactions, the busiest hour, message volumes per interface, database size and growth, batch job timings, and current uptime.\n- **The one real request:** an allow-listed IT analyst, at a hospital workstation, books and then cancels an appointment. It uses the production test patient (e.g. \"ZZTEST, PATIENT\") in a production test clinic. The confirmation appears on screen, the booking shows up in the on-prem app too (same database), and the interface engine sends the scheduling message to the EHR. The test patient must already be excluded from reminders and billing (ASSUMED; confirm with the interface team).\n- **Tiers it crosses:** workstation → hospital DNS and reverse proxy (routing flag by AD group) → IPsec VPN → private cloud load balancer → cloud app server VM (same version as on-prem) → back across the link to the on-prem database → on-prem interface engine → EHR.\n- **Deploy, log, monitor, roll back:**\n  - Terraform and app images go through the existing CI pipeline.\n  - Logs from the app, load balancer and VPN flows go to a log store classified as PHI and are forwarded to the SIEM, with one trace ID carried across tiers.\n  - A synthetic test-patient booking runs every 5 minutes and alerts on-call if it fails.\n  - Rollback: switch the proxy flag back to the on-prem servers, and redeploy the previous Terraform version. Both are exercised once.\n- **Who can reach it:** only the IT allow-list AD group. The connection to the production database is opened only after V1 passes. Everyone else stays on the on-prem servers.\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- The test booking succeeds with one trace across every tier.\n- A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline.\n- An injected failure (app VM stopped) fires the alert.\n- The network round-trip time and cloud-path latency are recorded as near-zero-load floors, not as capacity figures.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Network links, replication and pilot clinic**\n  - **Unlocks:** the decision on the coexistence sequence (V2) and the cutover design (V3).\n  - **Depends on:** V0 and V1.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Bring both private links live; test failover between them and to the VPN.\n    2. Start read-only replication from the on-prem database to the cloud database. This opens V3's 14-day window.\n    3. Use traces to count database calls per key transaction.\n    4. Route one low-acuity outpatient clinic's schedulers to the cloud app servers for V2.\n  - **Rollback:** switch the proxy flag back for the pilot. Stop replication and destroy the cloud copy, recording the deletion.\n  - **Exit check:** V2 and V3 pass.\n\n- **Phase 2: Interfaces ready; app-server waves**\n  - **Unlocks:** all users on the cloud app servers; a cutover-ready interface list.\n  - **Depends on:** V2 (for the waves) and V3 (for moving read-only users).\n  - **Tasks** (widest rework first):\n    1. Replace hard-coded database and app hostnames or IPs with DNS aliases in every consumer found.\n    2. Get the cloud outbound IPs onto partner allow-lists.\n    3. Test each interface in a cloud test environment with test data only. Drill holding and releasing message queues in the interface engine (V5).\n    4. Move read-only users (reporting ETL) to the cloud copy.\n    5. Move users in waves, at least 5 business days each: low-volume outpatient → high-volume outpatient → central call center → procedural, oncology and OR scheduling. A wave widens only when latency, error rate and help-desk tickets stay within the V2 bar.\n  - **If V2 failed:** step 5 is dropped and users stay on-prem until Phase 5.\n  - **Rollback:** proxy flag per wave; DNS aliases pointed back.\n  - **Exit check:** V5 passes, and every wave has held for 5 days.\n\n- **Phase 3: Cloud database capacity and resilience**\n  - **Unlocks:** cutover rehearsals and capacity commitments.\n  - **Depends on:** V3, plus the RTO/RPO and budget inputs.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Load test and failure drills for V4.\n    2. Set backup policy and test restores.\n    3. Run the downtime-report job from the cloud and confirm it prints at each site.\n    4. Set alerts on the cloud database (replication delay, blocking, storage).\n    5. Compare run cost to budget, then commit reserved capacity.\n  - **Rollback:** nothing is exposed; resize or re-tier the database.\n  - **Exit check:** V4 passes; run cost is within budget; on-call runbooks are updated.\n\n- **Phase 4: Cutover rehearsals and go/no-go**\n  - **Unlocks:** Phase 5.\n  - **Depends on:** V1–V5 and the \"no downtime\" definition.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Write the runbook (Phase 5 steps), the rollback triggers and the communications plan for staff and help desk.\n    2. Run at least two full rehearsals on a production-sized copy, each including a complete rollback (V6).\n    3. Put the change freeze in place.\n    4. Pick the lowest-volume window from the baseline.\n  - **Rollback:** nothing in production changes.\n  - **Exit check:** V6 passes, including the go/no-go signatures.\n\n- **Phase 5: Production cutover and stabilization**\n  - **Unlocks:** the cloud database as system of record.\n  - **Depends on:** V6.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Interface engine holds incoming admission/transfer and order queues.\n    2. App enters save-hold mode (ASSUMED the app supports this; otherwise the proxy returns a retry).\n    3. Wait for replication delay = 0 and confirm the log positions match.\n    4. Promote the cloud database to primary and start reverse replication to on-prem.\n    5. Switch the database DNS alias; release the interface queues.\n    6. Run a test-patient booking smoke test and reconciliation (row counts per table, plus a hash per appointment ID for the last 30 and next 365 days).\n    7. Go/no-go at T+15 minutes; reconcile again at T+1 h, T+24 h and T+7 days. A month-end batch must run in the cloud.\n  - **Rollback (available until V7):** fail back to on-prem using the reverse replication within 30 minutes. Triggers: any reconciliation difference not explained within 15 minutes; error rate above 2 × baseline for 10 minutes; an interface backlog that isn't draining.\n  - **Exit check:** zero reconciliation differences, reverse replication within budget, month-end completed.\n\n- **Phase 6: Decommission (point of no return)**\n  - **Unlocks:** retiring the on-prem servers.\n  - **Depends on:** V7.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Final archive export in an open format.\n    2. Stop reverse replication.\n    3. Remove the on-prem app servers from the proxy pool.\n    4. Wipe the media to NIST SP 800-88 and keep the certificates.\n  - **Rollback:** none after reverse replication stops. V7 guards this.\n  - **Exit check:** asset records are updated; the inventory shows no remaining connections to the old hosts.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | Phase 0 skeleton | The V0 exit check in §4 | Pipeline run records, trace export for the test patient, alert record | Phase 1 | 0 |\n| V1 | The cloud scope protects PHI before any PHI passes through it | BAA executed. Security risk analysis of the target design. Policy-as-code scan (Azure Policy / AWS Config) plus an external port scan. Review of the logging path | Sign-off by the HIPAA Security Officer, addressing 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1) (risk analysis), 164.308(b) (BAA) and 164.312 (technical safeguards) (REQUIREMENT). Zero public endpoints in scope. All storage encrypted with customer-managed keys. Audit logs arriving in the SIEM | Signed risk analysis, BAA reference, scan reports, kept in the GRC repository | Phase 0 connection to the production database; Phase 1 replication. If it fails: no PHI goes to the cloud; fix and re-review | Starts in 0; needed before the skeleton touches the production database |\n| V2 | App servers in the cloud with the database on-prem stay within the latency budget for real schedulers | Database calls per transaction × measured round-trip time as a forecast, then a 10-business-day pilot clinic | Each key transaction's p95 ≤ 1.2 × BASELINE p95 (ASSUMPTION). Error rate no higher than BASELINE. No severe tickets caused by the move | Latency dashboard export (no PHI), pilot ticket log | Phase 2 waves. If it fails: the coexistence sequence flips to a combined cutover | 1 |\n| V3 | The cloud copy stays complete and current | At least 14 days of replication covering a month-end and the nightly batch. It is not a small build: it handles patient health information (PHI), affects many teams and has outside interface partners.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness first (every appointment kept exactly once), then availability.\n- **Worst failure:** Appointments that are silently lost, duplicated or double-booked during coexistence or cutover. If scheduling is a module of the hospital's main health record system (EHR), it cannot be moved on its own.\n2. **How the client connects.** The plan assumes a 3-tier setup: a browser or Citrix-published client talks to app servers, which talk to the database. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\nPhase 0 is the thinnest real path through the new cloud setup, with the old system as the fallback:\n\n- **Start long-lead items on day one:** BAA, security risk analysis, vendor support statement, network link orders, partner allow-list requests, change board calendar, the \"no downtime\" definition, RTO/RPO and run-cost budget.\n- **List everything that depends on the system.** Sources: interface engine routes, 30+ days of database connection logs covering a month-end, firewall flow logs, SQL Agent and other scheduled jobs, DNS lookups. Record p95 for key transactions, the busiest hour, message volumes per interface, database size and growth, batch job timings, and current uptime.\n- **The one real request:** an allow-listed IT analyst, at a hospital workstation, books and then cancels an appointment. Use traces to count database calls per key transaction.\n    4. Route one low-acuity outpatient clinic's schedulers to the cloud app servers for V2.\n  - **Rollback:** switch the proxy flag back for the pilot. Move read-only users (reporting ETL) to the cloud copy.\n    5.
